problem.text: In the expression $(\underline{\quad}\times\underline{\quad})+(\underline{\quad}\times\underline{\quad})$ each blank is to be filled in with one of the digits $1$, $2$, $3$, or $4$, with each digit being used once. How many different values can be obtained?

steps.title: Where to start: ways to fill are not the same as values
steps.body: The question asks for different **values**, not different ways to fill the blanks. Many fillings give the same value, so the plan is to find which changes to a filling leave its value the same.

your_turn.prompt: How many ways are there to fill the four blanks with $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, each used once?
your_turn.answer: $24$, since $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$. Careful: this counts fillings, not values.

steps.title: Swaps that do not change the value
steps.body: Swapping the two numbers inside a product does not change it, since $a \times b = b \times a$. Swapping the two products does not change the sum either. Careful: if you divide out only the swaps inside each product, you still count some sums twice, because the two products can also trade places.

your_turn.prompt: Do $(2 \times 1) + (4 \times 3)$ and $(3 \times 4) + (1 \times 2)$ give the same value? Why?
your_turn.answer: Yes, both are $14$. They use the same two pairs, $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$, just in a different order.

steps.title: Only the pairs matter
steps.body: So the value depends only on how the four digits split into two pairs. Every split puts $1$ with some partner, and the other two digits form the second pair. Work out the value for each possible partner of $1$.

your_turn.prompt: What value do you get when $1$ is paired with $3$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
The partner of $1$ can be $2$, $3$, or $4$, and the three splits give
$$1 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 4 = 14, \quad 1 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4 = 11, \quad 1 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 3 = 10.$$
These are all different, so there are $3$ different values. The answer is **(B)**.

wrong_choices.E: $24$ is the number of ways to fill the blanks. Many of those fillings give the same value, so it counts too much.
wrong_choices.D: $6$ comes from dividing $24$ by $4$ for the swaps inside each product. The two products can also trade places, which gives the same sum, so each value is still counted twice.
